short: Collaborative combat aircraft: a jet-powered drone built to fly alongside a crewed fighter and take on risky jobs.
long: A collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) is a jet-powered drone designed to fly as a wingman to a crewed fighter like the F-35 or F-47. The pilot stays in the safer jet while the drone scouts ahead, jams enemy radar, carries extra missiles or acts as a decoy. CCAs cost a fraction of a fighter, so the Air Force can buy many and accept losing some. That changes the math of air combat from a few exquisite jets to many cheaper ones. Anduril's YFQ-44A and General Atomics' YFQ-42A were picked for the first round; later rounds decide which companies become long-term suppliers, which is why each award moves the industry.

short: First-person-view drone: a small, cheap drone flown through a live video feed, often used as a guided explosive.
long: An FPV (first-person-view) drone is a small quadcopter the operator flies by watching a live camera feed through goggles or a screen. Built from hobby parts, many cost a few hundred dollars, and armies strap explosives to them to hit tanks, trenches and vehicles with precision that used to need a missile. Ukraine and Russia each use millions a year, which turned drone production volume, cost per unit and resistance to jamming into deciding factors. For investors, FPVs show why the money is moving toward cheap, mass-produced systems and the factories that make them.

short: Unmanned aircraft system: a drone plus its ground control station and data links.
Uncrewed surface vessel: a boat that operates without a crew, remotely or on its own.
long: An uncrewed surface vessel (USV) is a boat with no one aboard. Some are small and fast, packed with explosives, like the sea drones Ukraine used to push Russia's Black Sea fleet back; others are long-endurance sailing or diesel craft that patrol, map the seabed or listen for submarines for months. Navies like them because a ship's crew is the most expensive and irreplaceable part. Companies such as Saildrone build these, and contracts for them are a growing share of naval spending.

short: Unmanned ground vehicle: a robot that drives on land to carry supplies, clear mines or fight.
A drone that circles over an area until it finds a target, then dives into it and explodes.
Systems that detect and stop enemy drones: jammers, interceptor drones, guns and lasers.
long: Counter-drone (or counter-UAS) means anything that finds and defeats hostile drones. It usually works in layers: radar and cameras to spot drones, jammers to cut their control link or GPS, and if that fails, something that physically stops them, such as guns, interceptor drones or lasers. The core problem is cost: shooting a $3,000 drone with a $1 million missile is a losing trade. That is why cheap interceptors and directed-energy weapons are among the fastest-growing areas of defense spending, and why Gulf states, Europe and US bases are all buying.

short: Weapons that use lasers or microwaves instead of bullets; each shot costs dollars, not millions.
A missile that flies at more than five times the speed of sound and can maneuver, making it hard to intercept.
long: A hypersonic missile travels faster than Mach 5, about a mile per second, and unlike a ballistic missile it can steer during flight. That combination of speed and maneuvering leaves defenders only seconds to react and makes the missile's path hard to predict. China and Russia have fielded some; the US is catching up with programs across the services and a wave of startups such as Castelion and Hermeus. Building them depends on heat-resistant materials and solid rocket motors, which is why those supply chains get so much investment attention.

short: The US plan for a nationwide missile-defense shield, with sensors and interceptors in space and on the ground.
long: Golden Dome is the Trump administration's plan to defend the whole United States against ballistic, hypersonic and cruise missiles. It layers satellites that detect and track launches, space-based interceptors that could strike missiles early in flight, and ground-based defenses like the Patriot and THAAD systems. Official estimates are around $175 to $185 billion, and independent ones run far higher. For the industry it is one of the largest new pools of money in decades, especially for satellite makers, space-sensor companies and missile-defense contractors, so awards under it are closely watched.

short: A Pentagon program to buy hundreds of thousands of cheap small drones fast, from many suppliers.
Space Development Agency: the Pentagon office buying large constellations of small military satellites in yearly batches (tranches).
Defense Innovation Unit: the Pentagon office that helps commercial tech companies win military contracts quickly.
The Pentagon's research agency that funds high-risk technology bets; it helped create the internet and GPS.
National Defense Authorization Act: the yearly law that sets US defense policy and spending limits (the money itself comes from appropriations).
A temporary law that keeps the government funded at last year's levels when Congress hasn't passed a budget; new programs usually can't start.
long: A continuing resolution (CR) is a stopgap law Congress passes when it hasn't agreed on the year's spending bills. It keeps agencies running at roughly last year's funding, but generally forbids starting new programs or increasing production. For defense companies that means planned contracts slip, sometimes for months. When the news says funding 'expires' on a date, it means the CR runs out and Congress must pass another one, pass full appropriations, or risk a shutdown. That's why CR deadlines show up on the calendar.

short: The laws that actually give agencies money to spend each year, separate from the laws that authorize programs.
Foreign military sales: the US government process for selling American weapons to allied governments.
A contract that sets a ceiling (say $500M) and lets the government order as needed; the headline number is a maximum, not money spent.
long: An IDIQ (indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity) contract is a framework deal. The government picks one or several companies and sets a maximum value and time period, then places individual orders as needs arise. So when a headline says a company won a '$500 million contract', it is often an IDIQ ceiling; the company may receive much less, and several companies may share the same ceiling. The real signal is in the first orders placed and how fast they follow. Reading awards this way keeps you from overestimating a win.

short: Other transaction authority: a faster way for the Pentagon to buy prototypes, outside normal procurement rules.
The biggest defense contractors (Lockheed Martin, RTX, Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, Boeing) that lead major programs.
The security pact between Australia, the UK and the US, covering nuclear submarines for Australia and shared advanced tech.
Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance: everything that collects information on an enemy, from satellites to drones.
Command and control: the software and networks commanders use to see the battlefield and direct forces.
long: Command and control (C2) is how a military turns information into decisions and orders. Today it is mostly software: systems that fuse data from satellites, drones, radars and troops into one picture, suggest targets and push orders back out. Whoever builds that layer becomes hard to replace, because every sensor and weapon has to plug into it. That's why Palantir's Maven and similar platforms are among the most valuable positions in defense tech, and why rules about open standards and data rights matter so much to investors.

short: Electronic warfare: jamming, spoofing and listening to radio signals to blind or confuse an enemy's radars, drones and communications.
The main US ground-based air and missile defense system; each PAC-3 interceptor costs several million dollars.
Lockheed Martin's stealth fighter, flown by the US and many allies; the largest weapons program in history.
The name the administration gave the Department of Defense in 2025 as a second title; news now uses both, and 'DOW' means the Pentagon.
The Pentagon office that lends money to companies building critical technology and supply chains in the US.
A government loan promise that becomes final only after the company meets set conditions, such as raising matching private money.
Venture funding rounds in order: Series A funds early growth, later letters fund scaling; each usually raises more at a higher valuation.
A shell company listed on a stock exchange that merges with a private company to take it public without a traditional IPO.
Orders a company has signed but not yet delivered; a large backlog means years of revenue already booked.
A contract awarded to one company without competition, usually because only it can do the work.
Metals used to make strong magnets for motors, missiles and drones; China dominates their mining and processing.
The engine in most missiles; only a few US makers exist, so shortages limit how fast missiles can be built.
A satellite that watches the ground; radar (SAR) versions can see through clouds and at night.
The interest rate on the most common US home loan, fixed for 30 years; Freddie Mac publishes the national average weekly.
long: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate is what most US homebuyers pay to borrow, locked for the life of the loan. Freddie Mac's weekly survey is the standard measure. It matters because the monthly payment moves a lot with it: on a $400,000 loan, going from 6% to 7% adds about $260 a month. Mortgage rates follow the 10-year Treasury yield more than the Fed's rate directly, so they react to inflation and economic news. For an investor, the rate sets your financing cost, which decides whether a rental's rent covers its payment.

short: A home loan paid off in 15 years: a lower rate and far less total interest, but a higher monthly payment.
Government-backed companies that buy most US mortgages from lenders, which keeps loans available; Freddie also publishes the weekly rate survey.
The interest rate on 10-year US government bonds; mortgage rates usually sit about 1.5 to 3 points above it.
The US central bank; it sets short-term rates, which influence mortgage rates indirectly through bond markets and inflation expectations.
How many homes are for sale; low inventory pushes prices up, rising inventory gives buyers more power.
long: Inventory is the number of homes listed for sale. It is one of the best signals of who has the upper hand. When few homes are for sale, buyers compete and prices rise; when listings pile up, sellers cut prices and buyers can negotiate. Analysts often turn it into 'months of supply': how long it would take to sell every listing at the current pace, with about six months seen as balanced. Since 2022 many owners with low mortgage rates have stayed put, keeping inventory tight, so changes in listings say a lot about where prices go next.

short: Homes under contract but not yet closed; a leading signal for sales a month or two ahead.
How many new homes construction began on in a month; a signal of future supply.
A widely cited index of US home prices, based on repeat sales of the same houses.
Zillow's estimate of the typical home's value in an area; ANU uses it for prices and price changes.
How hard it is to buy a home on a typical income, mostly driven by prices and mortgage rates together.
A year's rent divided by the home's price; a quick first test of whether a rental can pay for itself.
long: Rent yield (or gross yield) is a year of rent divided by the purchase price. A $250,000 home renting for $2,000 a month brings in $24,000 a year, a 9.6% gross yield. It ignores costs, so it is a first filter, not a final answer: taxes, insurance, repairs, vacancies and management often eat 40 to 50% of rent. Still, it is the fastest way to compare markets. Expensive coastal cities often yield 4 to 5%, while Midwest metros can yield 9% or more, which is why investors chasing cash flow look there.

short: Net operating income (rent minus operating costs, before the mortgage) divided by price; a cost-adjusted yield.
What a rental leaves you each month after all costs and the mortgage payment; negative means you pay in.
An investor loan approved on the property's rent covering its payment, rather than on your personal income.
A credit line borrowed against the equity in your home, usually at a variable rate.
A government-insured mortgage with low down payments (as little as 3.5%), popular with first-time buyers.
Adjustable-rate mortgage: a fixed rate for a few years, then it resets with the market, up or down.
Fees paid upfront to the lender to lower your mortgage rate; one point costs 1% of the loan.
Replacing a mortgage with a new one, usually to get a lower rate or pull out cash.
When a lender takes a home back because the owner stopped paying the mortgage.
The National Association of Realtors, the trade group that reports existing-home sales and median prices each month.
